body: {"total":5,"records":[{"title":"Hospital-initiated referral to housing first and subsequent emergency department use: a matched comparison","authors":"Mbeki-Carlsson T, Obi-Fairweather L, Soto-Lindqvist A","year":2022,"venue":"Silverbeck Inclusion Health Services","doi":"10.5555/jihs.2022.0151","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared 310 inpatients experiencing homelessness who were referred from hospital to a housing-first programme with 620 eligible inpatients who were not referred, matched on age, sex, number of admissions in the previous year and primary diagnosis group. Fifty-eight percent of referred patients were housed within six months. In the following year, referred patients made 6.1 emergency department visits per person against 8.4 among comparison patients, and had fewer emergency readmissions. Referred patients were more often known to the social work team before admission, so engagement with services may explain part of the difference."},{"title":"Referral pathways from acute hospitals to housing-first programmes: an interview study with social workers and housing staff","authors":"Kowalski-Adeyemi R, Lindgren-Achebe P","year":2020,"venue":"Hospital Social Work Research Notes","doi":"10.5555/swhcr.2020.0083","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We interviewed 21 hospital social workers and 14 housing-first staff in two cities about referrals made during a hospital admission. Referrals failed most often because identity documents or income details were missing, because the patient was discharged before the housing team could meet them, or because housing staff could not reach the patient after discharge. Social workers who knew a named housing worker referred more often and more completely. Both groups asked for a shared referral form, an agreed contact after discharge and a way for housing staff to visit the ward."},{"title":"Housing-first programme outcomes by referral source: annual report of a city programme","authors":"City Housing First Partnership","year":2023,"venue":"City Housing First Partnership annual reports","providerType":"report","abstract":"This annual report describes 1,020 referrals to a city housing-first programme. Referrals from hospitals were accepted less often than referrals from street outreach teams (41 against 63 percent), mainly because hospital referral forms were incomplete or the person could not be contacted after discharge. Among people who were housed, tenancy sustainment at 12 months was 81 percent and did not differ by referral source. The report gives no information on health service use and does not describe how acceptance decisions were made."},{"title":"Referral selection in observational evaluations of housing programmes: eligible non-referred comparators and negative control outcomes","authors":"Haddad-Pereira J, Nkemelu-Voss S","year":2019,"venue":"Methods in Health and Housing Research","doi":"10.5555/mhhr.2019.0027","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"People referred to housing programmes differ from those who are not referred in engagement, health and support, so simple comparisons overstate benefits. Using two linked datasets, we compared strategies for choosing a comparison group. Eligible non-referred people matched on previous service use and weighted by propensity scores gave estimates closer to those from a randomised evaluation than unmatched comparisons. A negative control outcome, planned outpatient attendance, helped detect residual confounding by engagement. We recommend defining eligibility identically for both groups and measuring engagement before the index admission."},{"title":"Trust, consent and data linkage with people experiencing homelessness: a participatory study","authors":"Osei-Brennan M, Castellanos-Holm D, Tanaka-Mwangi F","year":2024,"venue":"Pellmoor Participatory Health Research","doi":"10.5555/jphr.2024.0106","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Peer researchers with lived experience of homelessness led group discussions with 46 people about taking part in research that links health and housing data. Most were willing to allow linkage if they could decide what was linked, if data would never be shared with police, immigration or benefits agencies, and if results came back to them. Participation was higher when a peer researcher explained the study and when a small payment was offered for interviews. People described earlier research that had taken their stories and given nothing back. The authors recommend layered consent and a community advisory group."}]}
